title: IBM supports award-winning projects in NEDO Quantum Challenge
content: Quantum Research Blog IBM supports award-winning projects in NEDO Quantum Challenge Teams in all three tracks of Japan’s national quantum competition used IBM quantum computers during their research, with projects ranging from disaster prevention and the gut microbiome to anime production. Date 23 Oct 2026 Authors Chris Nay Toru Imai (今井 亨) Yuri Kobayashi Topics Community Network Share this blog Was this blog post helpful? Yes No Key takeaways: All nine prize-winning teams used IBM quantum computers during their research for the NEDO Quantum Challenge. Winning projects spanned all three tracks: Society 5.0, Quality of Life, and Cool Japan. Teams explored applications including disaster prevention, drug discovery, gut microbiome analysis, materials research, music generation, and animation. IBM supported participants with quantum computing resources, technical guidance, workshops, and access to educational content. When Japan’s New Energy and Industrial Technology Development Organization (NEDO) presented the first-season awards of its NEDO Quantum Challenge on 15 October 2026, winning teams across the competition’s Society 5.0, Quality of Life (QoL) and Cool Japan tracks reported results generated on IBM quantum hardware. In fact, all nine prize-winning teams used IBM quantum computers during their research for the challenge, and six of them relied on IBM quantum computers exclusively. Each topic track had at least one winner that ran exclusively on IBM quantum computers. Winning projects ranged from disaster prevention, transaction security, and microbiome design to music generation and manga production. Two winning teams that used IBM quantum computers have already launched companies based on their work: Q4Health and EntangleTune. IBM’s support went beyond quantum computer access. Throughout the challenge, IBM gave participants access to five of the company’s quantum computers with its latest processors, along with education, hands-on programming sessions, personalized Quantum Clinic consultations and technical support. IBM experts also advised Society 5.0 third-place winning team, Setouchi kara Ryoshi no Sekai e, on its algorithm, and joined Cool Japan third-place winning team with Mitsubishi Chemical, Keio University, and Arizona State University as co-researchers. Quantum computing for real-world problems NEDO, which operates under Japan’s Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry, launched the prize-based program to explore how next-generation quantum computers could address societal issues and to quickly identify promising early-stage technologies that could give rise to new industries. Teams were asked to tackle problems that are difficult or impossible for today’s computers. The competition organized those problems into three tracks: Society 5.0 projects explored problems related to infrastructure safety, trustworthy transactions and vehicle design as part of Japan’s broader initiative to use advanced technologies to address societal challenges. Quality of Life projects focused on health, including drug discovery, multidrug-resistant infections and the gut microbiome. Cool Japan projects applied quantum computing to areas ranging from music and anime production to low-carbon chemical manufacturing. Each track offered prizes of ¥40 million (about $270,000) for first place, ¥20 million (about $130,000) for second and ¥10 million (about $67,000) for third. Season 1, which began research and development in fiscal year 2025, drew 87 applications. Judges awarded nine prizes: the QoL track awarded first, second and third place, while Society 5.0 and Cool Japan each awarded one second-place and two third-place prizes, with no first prize, due to the high benchmarks required in each track. IBM was among a few organizations that provided computing environments to participants free of charge, and IBM Quantum became the most widely selected platform: 65 of the 80 participating teams, about 81%, chose IBM. Those teams ran 11,159 jobs and used more than 5,900 minutes of quantum compute time, about 105% of the allocated time, with activity surging in the final month before the June 30 submission deadline. Society 5.0: safer infrastructure, trusted transactions and lighter cars In the Society 5.0 track, NV Learning Center won second place with a project to improve infrastructure safety and disaster prevention. The team applied quantum Krylov learning and quantum state transfer, running its final results entirely on IBM quantum computers. Q-Chainners took third place by combining a quantum hash function with classical processing to make transactions more trustworthy. The team ran its final results on four different IBM quantum computers. Setouchi kara Ryoshi no Sekai e also placed third with a car-body design project aimed at making vehicles lighter.
